The garden has had quite a year. Here are some of the notes.

## Beans

The runner beans climbed past the top of the frame by July. We tied them to the fence with old string, and they kept going until the flowers turned the whole corner red. The bees found them in a day. By August we were picking every morning and giving bags away to anyone who walked past the gate.

Planting them two weeks later than last year was a gamble but it paid off. The late frost in May missed them completely, and the soil was warm enough that they came up in five days.

## Tomatoes

This year I went from four plants to eleven across three beds. Some were from seed, some were gifts from the neighbour, and two came up on their own in the compost heap. The cherry ones did best by far. The big beefsteaks split after the heavy rain in August, and I learned that watering less in the last weeks makes them sweeter.

I’ve really enjoyed trying new varieties and watching which ones like this corner of the yard. The yellow pear tomato is staying on the list for next year.

## Shed

Last spring the shed roof finally gave up. I spent two weekends stripping the old felt, replacing three rotten boards, and nailing on new sheets. It isn’t pretty, but it’s dry. Inside I built a narrow shelf for seed packets and a rack for the hoes and rakes so they stop falling over every time the door opens. The old potting table went to a friend who wanted it for her own garden.

I’m planning to paint it next year, but I’m not sure what colour. A few options I’m thinking about:

* A deep green that disappears into the hedge, so the shed feels like part of the garden
* A pale blue like the old boat house at the end of the lane, which looks good in winter
* A plain white that keeps it cool in summer and makes the tools easier to find in the dark

## Compost

This year has been the second year the compost has worked properly. It finally turned dark and crumbly instead of slimy, and it smells like a forest floor.

The trick was adding more brown material: shredded cardboard, dry leaves, and the straw from the rabbit hutch. Turning it every two weeks helped too. By September I had enough to spread a thick layer over every bed, and the worms moved in by the hundreds as soon as it went down.

## Watering

This year I finally set up a rain barrel by the shed. I’m really pleased with how much it saves, though it ran dry twice in the hot weeks.

I’ve noticed a big change in how I water. I used to stand with the hose every evening. Now I water deeply twice a week at the roots, and the plants seem stronger for it. The lawn went brown in August, but it came back green within a week of the first rain.

I am also learning how to balance the garden with everything else. There are weeks when it gets away from me, and the weeds win for a while. That is fine. A garden forgives a lot if you come back to it, and the beds were tidy again by the end of the month.

## Seeds

This year we saved seeds from the beans, the tomatoes, and the marigolds. In total it was about forty little paper envelopes, labelled in pencil and stored in a biscuit tin in the cool cupboard under the stairs. I gave half of them away at the village swap in October and came home with packets of kale, chard, and a strange purple carrot.

On average a saved packet holds about thirty seeds, which is far more than I need. The rest go to friends, to the school garden, and to the little seed library box that someone set up next to the bus stop.

## Weeds

This year the bindweed came back from the corner by the fence, as it does every year. I pulled it every week from May to September. It wraps around everything it touches: the beans, the fence, the handle of a fork left out overnight. The roots go down deeper than any spade can reach, and every small piece that breaks off grows into a new plant by the following week. I have stopped hoping to win and settled for keeping it out of the vegetable beds.

It’s become such a normal part of the garden that I don’t mind it much anymore. Pulling it is quiet work, and it gives me a reason to be out there early in the morning when the birds are loud and the light is low. I found a frog under the leaves one day and a hedgehog the next. Some weeks the weeding is the best hour of the day.

## Birds

It’s been lovely to see more birds this year. The feeder by the kitchen window has had blue tits, goldfinches, a pair of robins, and once a woodpecker who stayed for a whole morning and left the peanut tray empty.

The robins nested in the ivy on the shed wall and raised two broods. We watched the young ones learn to fly from the shed roof to the apple tree and back again.

In many ways, the birds keep the garden in balance. They eat the aphids on the roses and the caterpillars on the cabbages.
